summary: Elizabeth Lopatto argues in The Verge that Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial could damage the entire crypto industry, depending on what evidence emerges. The piece outlines the seven charges, the government's likely case on intent and witnesses, and how the defense might implicate investors, Binance, and industry peers. Bankman-Fried's earlier media-savvy persona and his wild-card behavior add to the uncertainty.
one_line: Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX fraud trial could harm the whole crypto industry through evidence, witness testimony, and defense strategy, not just determine his own guilt.
key_facts: Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of FTX and Alameda Research, faces seven criminal counts: two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy counts.
FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019; the SEC alleges it was a fraud "from the start," diverting customer funds to Alameda.

John J. Ray III, who cleaned up Enron, now leads what's left of FTX and called the conduct "really just old-fashioned embezzlement"; FTX lawyers sued Bankman-Fried's parents to recover millions of dollars.
A superseding indictment filed August 14th says FTX code features "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction.
Bankman-Fried is accused of using misappropriated customer deposits to help buy more than $200 million of real estate, make investments for himself, and repay Alameda's lenders.
He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds for political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of these though they are not part of the charges.
A second trial with additional charges is scheduled for March 2024.
Prosecutors must first show transactions took place, then connect them to Bankman-Fried and prove he knew it was wrong and lied; Christopher LaVigne says this second part is where the drama lies.
The indictment calls Bankman-Fried's November 2022 tweets "false and misleading," and his own words may be used to establish intent.

Likely witnesses include Caroline Ellison, Gary Wang, and Nishad Singh, who plead guilty or are cooperating; Bankman-Fried was jailed for witness tampering after leaking Ellison's diaries to The New York Times.
Investors such as Sequoia Capital and early investor Binance may have people called to testify about what Bankman-Fried told them.
Hermine Wong warns Bankman-Fried might argue "Everyone was doing this," or introduce crypto group chat messages, which could damage public perception of crypto.
Before his arrest, Bankman-Fried planned to bring group chat messages into congressional testimony blaming Binance and Sullivan & Cromwell.
Bankman-Fried's lawyers argue his constitutional rights are violated by pretrial incarceration, citing a poor internet connection for planning his defense, which could be grounds for appeal.
